BASIC SCIENCE

Rheumatology

Original article

Rheumatology 2023;62:886–893 https://doi.org/10.1093/rheumatology/keac253 Advance access publication 23 April 2022

Strong site-specific association of pharyngeal cultures with the onset of psoriatic arthritis and psoriasis, regardless of pathogen

Telma Thrastardottir 1, Elana Meer 2, Arna Hauksdottir 1,3, Bjorn Gudbjornsson 1,4, Sigurdur Yngvi Kristinsson 1,5, Alexis Ogdie 6,7

and Thorvardur Jon Love 1,8

Abstract

Objectives. The objective of this study was to evaluate any association between culture site / culture result / pathogen and incident PsA or psoriasis. Methods. Records of all samples sent for culture from a large population during a 3-year period were linked with nationwide registry data on diagnoses and death over a 15-year period. The main outcomes of interest were incident diagnoses of PsA and psoriasis, deﬁned by International Classiﬁcation of Diseases (ICD) codes. The effect of culture site, culture result (positive vs negative), and pathogen (Streptococcus vs negative culture) on the risk of developing PsA and psoriasis was calculated using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age and gender. Results. A total of 313 235 bacterial cultures from 128 982 individuals were analysed. Comparing individuals with pharyngeal cultures to those with urine cultures, the hazard ratio for incident PsA was 8.78 [95% conﬁdence inter-val (CI) 3.23, 23.91] and for incident psoriasis it was 8.00 (95% CI 5.28, 12.12). Most of the risk was concentrated in the ﬁrst 50 days after the culture date. Increased risk was also found when comparing individuals with cultures from the pharynx with those with cultures from the nasopharynx and blood. An association with streptococci was not found, neither in the pharynx nor at any other site. A positive bacterial culture from any site was associated with reduced risk for both PsA and psoriasis. Conclusion. There is a strong site-speciﬁc association between pharyngeal culture samples and an increased risk of PsA and psoriasis, regardless of the pathogen. This may indicate that the site of infection, rather than the pathogen, is associated with increased risk.

Key words: psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis, infection, and risk factors

Rheumatology key messages

. There is a strong site-speciﬁc association between pharyngeal culture samples and an increased risk of PsA and psoriasis, regardless of the pathogen.

. Streptococcal infections were associated with neither psoriasis nor PsA.

. This may indicate that the site of infection, rather than the pathogen, is associated with increased risk.

Introduction

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease affect-ing 2–3% of the population. PsA is a closely related inflammatory arthritis that up to 30% of psoriasis patients develop [1]. These autoimmune diseases have a significant impact on health-related quality of life [2]. They share several genetic and environmental risk factors, and it has been suggested that psoriasis patients with predisposing genetic risk factors are at higher risk of developing PsA after exposure to an environmental trig-ger such as infection [3, 4]. Most previous studies have focused on the association between infection and psoriatic skin disease rather than the arthritis, but small sample sizes and study designs have limited all these studies. We have published a systematic review of the available literature on this topic. While the data were inconclusive, certain trends emerged suggesting areas that merit further study. This includes the role of streptococcal pharyngeal and laryngopharyngeal infections [5]. Of note, tonsils from psoriasis patients are more frequently colonized with bacteria than tonsils from individuals without the skin disease [6]. Moreover, previous studies have found an association of sore throat and streptococcal throat infections with exacerbation of psoriasis [7, 8]. In a study of 275 psoriasis patients, sore throat was associated with psoriasis exacerbation in 42% of patients with plaque psoriasis, 67% of patients with guttate psoriasis, and 70% of patients with both guttate and plaque psoriasis [8]. Of 140 patients with a confirmed streptococcal pharyngeal infection, 75% reported exacerbation. Further, tonsillectomy was found to be beneficial to those plaque psoriasis patients who reported streptococcal-associated exacerbation [9]. Whether the same applies to PsA remains unclear, but a recent case series describes three cases of acute onset of psoriatic SpA within 7–10 days of confirmed streptococcal throat infection [10]. In all three cases, antibiotics were given for a short period. Therefore, it is essential to study the association between infections and psoriatic disease in a large population-based cohort, paying particular attention to pharyngeal infections and streptococcal infections. The aim of this cohort study was to evaluate the association of infections with the onset of PsA and psoriasis by comparing the effect of site of infection and individual infectious agents on the risk of later developing the psoriatic disease.

Methods

In this population-based cohort study, data were obtained on all samples sent for bacterial culture in the Stockholm region of Sweden processed at Karolinska laboratories in Solna from 1 January 2004 until 31 December 2006. These included inpatient cultures as well as cultures from ambulatory patients and primary care patients in Northern Stockholm, where 1 million

Strong site-specific association of pharyngeal cultures

individuals reside. The data were linked to the Swedish Cause of Death Register and the Swedish National Patient Register, with inpatient diagnoses from 1 January 1994 through 31 December 2009, and outpatient diagnoses from 1 January 2001, through 31 December 2009. The Swedish National Inpatient Register has complete national coverage since 1987, and because of long follow-up it is very suitable for large-scale population-based studies. The validation rate is high for many diagnoses, and studies have suggested that the overall positive predictive value (PPV) of diagnosis is about 85–95% [11]. Accurate diagnosis of PsA is difficult in clinical practice but the validity of clinical diagnoses for PsA in the Swedish National Patient Register is good, with a single code having a positive predictive value of 86% for the fulfilment of PsA classification criteria [12]. This is similar to the PPV of 85% reported for a single diagnostic code for PsA diagnosis in the United Kingdom Health Improvement Network (THIN) [13]. In a study specifically focusing on the validation of RA diagnoses in the Swedish National Patient Register, the validity was found to be high or around 90% for prevalent RA and new-onset RA [14]. Individuals under the age of 18 were excluded. Personal identifiers were removed before data analysis.

Exposure

We used three separate definitions of exposure. First, the role of the site was explored by categorizing those individuals who had a sample sent for culture from their pharynx as exposed and those who had a urine, nasopharynx or blood sample as unexposed. This definition of exposure was based on the presumption that the de-cision to send a sample for culture was in most cases a surrogate for clinical symptoms at the site chosen for culture, i.e. symptoms of throat infection when a sample from the pharynx was sent for culture, symptoms of urinary tract infection when a urine sample was sent, etc. Second, the role of streptococci was explored by categorizing those with a pharyngeal culture positive for streptococci as exposed and those with a negative culture from the same site as unexposed. As an extension of this exploration, we categorized those with streptococci cultured from any site as exposed and those with a negative culture as unexposed. Finally, we explored the role of infection in general by categorizing those with positive pharyngeal culture as exposed and those with a negative pharyngeal culture as unexposed. In addition, we categorized all those with a positive culture from any site as exposed and those with a negative culture as unexposed.

Outcomes

Outcomes were defined based on the occurrence of a single recorded International Classification of Diseases (ICD) 10 diagnostic code compatible with psoriasis and PsA, shown in Supplementary Table S1 (available at

Rheumatology online). For our sensitivity analysis, we used a single code for RA. All ICD10 diagnostic codes listed in Supplementary Table S1 (available at Rheumatology online) were used in the analysis. The outcome data cover all of Sweden, so that while the exposure was only recorded in northern Stockholm, outcomes were captured wherever they were recorded in Sweden. To avoid counting prevalent disease in our analysis, individuals were excluded if the outcome of interest occurred at any time before the culture date or if it occurred during the first 7 days after the culture date. The latter exclusion was to minimize the possibility of including individuals who already had the outcome but received the diagnosis when being seen in connec-tion with the symptoms leading to a culture being obtained.

Follow-up

The index date for each individual was the date of the culture. Follow-up was concluded at the first occurrence of one of the following: 1000 days had passed, a new sample was received for culture, an outcome of interest was observed, death, or the study period ended. The follow-up period was set to 1000 days to allow time for a diagnostic delay, while still being credibly connected to the exposure of interest. When the same individual had multiple samples sent for culture from the same site within 30 days, they were treated as one exposure, using the date of the first sample as the index date, and they were considered positive if any sample was positive. In the case of multiple culture sites or different organisms being reported within 30 days, none were used in the analysis.

Sensitivity analysis

To test our findings for evidence of bias resulting from our design choices, we performed multiple sensitivity analyses by running the models with the following changes: (1) comparing pharynx cultures with all other culture sites, (2) including the first 7 days after culture date, (3) including only the first 7 days after culture date, and (4) following exposures for as long as the data would allow rather than the maximum of 1000 days. Finally, we included RA in all analyses to understand whether any observed effects applied to arthritis in general or were specific to psoriatic disease.

Statistical analysis

Cox proportional hazards models were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) for exposed vs unexposed groups. Each model was adjusted for age and gender. All models were tested for the proportional hazards model assumptions. When a model violated the proportional hazards assumption, the follow-up time was split into shorter periods. A visual inspection of Kaplan–Meier curves was used to determine where to split the time frame of the analysis. All data manipulation and statistical analyses were performed using JMP, R, and RStudio.

Ethical approval

Ethical approval was granted by the Regional Ethical Review Board in Stockholm (2007/1307–31/5).

Results

The dataset consisted of 2 017 413 bacterial cultures from 592 835 individuals, all submitted between 1 January 2004 and 31 December 2006. The most common culture types/sites were urine (47%), nasopharynx (23%), blood (14%) and pharynx (12%). The remaining culture types/ sites each had a prevalence under 2%. Cultures were positive in 693 891 cases (34%), and the pathogens found in 5% or more of samples were Escherichia coli (29%), Streptococcus species (19%), Haemophilus species (10%), Moraxella species (9%), Staphylococcus species (8%), Enterococcus species (8%) and Klebsiella species (5%). Of the 592 835 individuals, 62% were women. The gender discrepancy was mainly driven by the gender discrepancy in urine cultures, with 76% coming from women. The nasopharyngeal, pharyngeal and blood cultures had more equal gender ratios, with 56%, 57% and 47% coming from women. Following the exclusions, described in the Methods section and shown in Fig. 1, the results of 313 235 bacterial cultures from 128 982 individuals remained. Details regarding these samples and individuals are presented in Table 1. Based on visual inspection of Kaplan–Meier curves, the follow-up time was split after 50 days, and HRs were calculated for days 8–50, 51–1000 and for the whole period from 8–1000 days. The results of fully adjusted Cox model analyses with their HRs for incident PsA, psoriasis and RA by site, pathogen, and positive or negative culture result for each of these three periods are shown in Table 2. Sensitivity analyses showed that when pharyngeal cultures were compared with all other culture sites, a HR of 9.51 for PsA and 5.80 for psoriasis was seen in the first 50days. During the first 7days after culture, 207 individuals were diagnosed with psoriasis, including 151 on the same day as the culture was sent, as were 4 PsA cases and 79 RA cases. This high number of new psoriasis cases in such a short period led to a violation of the proportional hazard assumptions when the first week was included in the sensitivity analysis (data not shown). Likewise, when only the first 7days were analysed, some models for psoriasis violated the proportional hazard assumptions. During the first 7days the number of PsA and RA cases was too small to construct reliable models. When the follow-up time was extended to include all data rather than just the first 1000days, the results were not materially different from those shown for the primary analysis.

Discussion

In this population-based cohort study, having a pharyngeal sample sent for culture was strongly associated

Strong site-specific association of pharyngeal cultures

FIG. 1 Flow diagram of exclusions of cultures and the resulting datasets, and speciﬁc datasets for each outcome

with increased risk of psoriatic disease, both PsA and psoriasis. However, streptococcal infections were neither associated with psoriasis nor PsA. Having a positive pharyngeal culture was strongly protective for PsA and, to a lesser degree, protective for psoriasis. Importantly, none of these associations were present for RA. While this is the first study to examine throat cultures as a proxy for pharyngitis regardless of culture results, previous studies have found associations between streptococcal throat infection and psoriatic disease [7, 8, 10, 15, 16]. The risk increase associated with pharyngeal cultures was strongest compared with urine cultures, with a HR of 8.78 for PsA and 8.00 for psoriasis in the first 50 days after culture. Beyond 50 days, the increased risk persisted for PsA but with a lower HR. The increased HR was also present when comparing pharyngeal cultures to nasopharyngeal or blood cultures. In contrast to previous studies, there was no association between cultures positive for streptococci and psoriasis, neither from pharyngeal cultures nor other sites. Two possible explanations are the use of antibiotics in those patients who had a positive culture, or the sample size. Unfortunately, we did not have information on antibiotic use. The same reasons might explain the protective effects of a positive outcome of cultures from any site, with a HR of 0.34 for PsA in the first 50 days

after culture date and 0.66 for psoriasis in the first 50 days after culture date, but the protection against psoriasis had vanished 50 days after the culture date. These findings should be interpreted with caution and must be studied further before they can be generalized, in part because of the small number of positive Streptococcus infections, particularly in the case of PsA. Streptococcus is the most common bacteria causing pharyngitis and is treatable with antibiotics. However, most pharyngitis cases are caused by viruses such as coronavirus, adenovirus, influenza virus, Epstein-Barr virus, and others [17]. Therefore, most cases of pharyngitis do not lead to positive bacterial culture and are not treated with antibiotics. Therefore, negative pharyngeal cultures in our dataset may often represent individuals with symptoms of pharyngitis caused by viruses. New insights into the role of viral infections in the pathogenesis of SpA diseases such as PsA were presented in a recent study. The study included 18 PsA patients with a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis and showed that SARS-CoV-2 virus infections, which stimulate the TLR7 path-ways, resulted in flares of PsA and enthesis 12–23 days after infection [18]. In particular, the PsA flares were linked with activation of entheseal plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) and upregulation of TNF/IFN-a. These data suggest an important role of innate immunity in the development of PsA, which may be only partly pathogen

dependent. While previous studies on psoriasis have mainly focused on streptococcal pharyngitis, our results suggest that pharyngitis, regardless of the pathogen type, is associated with increased risk. This may be difficult to explore further in existing datasets, as viral cultures and/or PCR are far less frequently performed than bacterial cultures, making the approach presented here of focusing on the fact that a culture was needed, rather than its result, the best strategy to explore this question currently available in the population setting. The strengths of the study include the large number of cultures included and the completeness of the population-based follow-up data. Because the dataset used for outcome evaluation went as far back as 1994, the chance of including pre-existing disease was low. Whether the 207 psoriasis cases diagnosed during the first week had undiagnosed psoriasis before the culture date is unclear. According to results from NHANES 2003–2004, the prevalence of undiagnosed active psoriasis was 0.4–2.28% in the US population, aged 20– 59 years of age [19]. Likewise, it is uncertain whether the four PsA cases diagnosed during the first week after culture date had pre-existing but undiagnosed PsA, because the prevalence of undiagnosed PsA among

psoriasis patients is 15.5% [20]. We attempted to ad-just for this uncertainty by excluding the first week after the culture date from our primary analysis. As the data do not include information on other risk factors or the use of antibiotics, it will be necessary to use other data sources to perform studies that comple-ment these results. However, we adjusted for age and gender, which are important factors in autoimmune disease risk. Regarding streptococcal pharyngitis, it should be kept in mind that only beta-hemolytic streptococci group A, C or G are usually tested for in pharyngeal cultures. Other streptococci, such as alpha-streptococci, Group B Streptococcus, enterococci, and pneumococci, are usually not tested for in pharyngeal cultures. Since the exposure information was gathered from all cultures performed during a defined period of time from a single region of Sweden, they did not include information on whether the individual was hospitalized at the time. Therefore, we were unable to perform separate subanalyses of inpatient infections and outpatient infections. Finally, it is unclear whether the observed associations apply to less severe pharyngeal infections, since our dataset included information on pharyngeal cultures, which are sent only in those cases where symptoms

were severe enough for individuals to seek medical care and the physician considered the symptoms severe enough to warrant sampling for culture. In conclusion, a strong, site-specific association of pharyngitis with increased risk of PsA and psoriasis was found, regardless of pathogen type. This association was not seen for RA. While previous studies have focused on streptococcal pharyngitis, we found an association with a surrogate marker of clinically significant pharyngitis regardless of the pathogen. Further studies are needed to understand this association with pharyngitis more clearly, including analysing the role of antibiotic use and individual viral pathogens.
